title: Metals and Non-metals
description: Grade 7 Chemistry: Metals and Non-metals — concept notes, solved examples, key-point recaps, per-topic quizzes and free online tests.

topics.title: Physical Properties of Metals and Non-metals
topics.concept:
All the elements found in nature can be broadly divided into two large groups: metals and non-metals. They are told apart first by their physical properties — that is, properties we can observe without changing the substance chemically, such as appearance, hardness, and conductivity. Most metals share a set of typical physical properties, while non-metals generally show the opposite.

Metals usually have these physical properties: they have a shiny surface called metallic lustre (e.g. polished gold and silver); they are hard (except sodium and potassium, which are soft); they are malleable, meaning they can be beaten into thin sheets without breaking; they are ductile, meaning they can be drawn into thin wires; they are good conductors of heat and electricity; they are sonorous, meaning they produce a ringing sound when struck; and most metals have high melting and boiling points. Familiar metals include iron, copper, aluminium, gold, and silver.

Non-metals generally show the opposite physical properties: they are usually dull (not lustrous), soft or brittle (solids break easily into pieces), and are poor conductors of heat and electricity (they are insulators). They are not malleable or ductile, and they are not sonorous. Non-metals can be solids (like sulphur and carbon), liquids (bromine is the only liquid non-metal), or gases (like oxygen, nitrogen, and hydrogen). Examples of non-metals include oxygen, carbon, sulphur, and chlorine.

There are some interesting exceptions that make the picture richer. Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature; sodium and potassium are metals soft enough to be cut with a knife. Among non-metals, graphite (a form of carbon) is a good conductor of electricity, and diamond (another form of carbon) is the hardest known natural substance. Knowing these typical properties and exceptions lets us identify whether a material is a metal or a non-metal and helps explain why each is used as it is.

examples.problem: Example 1: A solid material is shiny, can be drawn into wires, conducts electricity, and rings when struck. Is it a metal or a non-metal?
examples.solution:
Match the properties to a group.

  • Being shiny (lustrous), ductile, a good conductor, and sonorous are all typical metallic properties.
  • Non-metals are dull, brittle, and poor conductors.
  • Answer: It is a metal, because it shows the typical physical properties of metals.
examples.answer: It is a metal, because it shows the typical physical properties of metals.

examples.problem: Example 2: What is meant by saying a metal is "malleable" and "ductile"?
examples.solution:
Define each property.

  • Malleable means the metal can be beaten into thin sheets without breaking.
  • Ductile means it can be drawn out into thin wires.
  • Answer: Malleable means it can be hammered into sheets, and ductile means it can be drawn into wires.
examples.answer: Malleable means it can be hammered into sheets, and ductile means it can be drawn into wires.

examples.problem: Example 3: Name a metal that is liquid at room temperature and a non-metal that conducts electricity.
examples.solution:
Recall the special exceptions.

  • Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.
  • Graphite, a form of carbon, is a non-metal that conducts electricity.
  • Answer: Mercury is the liquid metal, and graphite is the non-metal that conducts electricity.
examples.answer: Mercury is the liquid metal, and graphite is the non-metal that conducts electricity.

recap:
• Elements are divided into metals and non-metals, told apart first by their physical properties.
  • Metals are usually lustrous, hard, malleable, ductile, sonorous, and good conductors of heat and electricity, with high melting points.
  • Non-metals are usually dull, brittle or soft, non-sonorous, and poor conductors (insulators), and may be solid, liquid, or gas.
  • Examples: metals — iron, copper, aluminium, gold; non-metals — oxygen, carbon, sulphur, chlorine.
  • Key exceptions: mercury is a liquid metal; sodium and potassium are soft metals; graphite conducts; diamond is the hardest natural substance.

quiz.explanation: Ductility is the property of being drawn into wires; malleability is being beaten into sheets.

quiz.q: Most non-metals are ______ of heat and electricity.
quiz.explanation: Most non-metals are poor conductors (insulators) of heat and electricity.

quiz.explanation: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.

quiz.q: The ringing sound produced by metals when struck is due to the property called:
quiz.explanation: Producing a ringing sound on being struck is the property of sonorousness.

quiz.q: Which non-metal is a good conductor of electricity?
quiz.explanation: Graphite, a form of carbon, is an unusual non-metal that conducts electricity.

topics.title: Chemical Properties of Metals
topics.concept:
Besides their physical properties, metals are recognised by how they behave in chemical reactions — their chemical properties. Metals react with oxygen, water, and acids in characteristic ways, though different metals react with different vigour. Studying these reactions helps us understand corrosion, the extraction of metals, and many everyday processes.

Reaction with oxygen: Metals react with oxygen (usually on heating) to form metal oxides. For example, magnesium burns in air with a bright white flame to form magnesium oxide, and copper forms a black coating of copper oxide on heating. Importantly, metal oxides are basic in nature — they turn red litmus blue and react with acids. Some metal oxides, like those of aluminium and zinc, can behave as both acid and base and are called amphoteric, but the general rule is that metal oxides are basic.

Reaction with water: Metals react with water (or steam) to form metal hydroxides or oxides and release hydrogen gas, but the vigour varies greatly. Very reactive metals like sodium and potassium react violently even with cold water, so they must be stored under kerosene oil to keep them away from air and moisture. Less reactive metals like iron react only slowly or with steam, and some metals like gold do not react with water at all.

Reaction with acids: Most metals react with dilute acids to form a salt and release hydrogen gas, which burns with a "pop" sound. For example, zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to give zinc chloride and hydrogen. However, very unreactive metals like gold and silver do not react with dilute acids. The differing reactivity of metals is summarised in the reactivity series, an arrangement of metals from most reactive (like potassium and sodium) to least reactive (like silver and gold). A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from its salt solution. These chemical properties explain why some metals tarnish or corrode quickly while others, like gold, stay shiny for centuries.

examples.problem: Example 1: When magnesium burns in air, what type of compound is formed, and what is its nature with litmus?
examples.solution:
Recall the reaction with oxygen.

  • Magnesium reacts with oxygen to form magnesium oxide, a metal oxide.
  • Metal oxides are basic, so they turn red litmus blue.
  • Answer: Magnesium oxide (a metal oxide) is formed, and it is basic, turning red litmus blue.
examples.answer: Magnesium oxide (a metal oxide) is formed, and it is basic, turning red litmus blue.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why are sodium and potassium stored under kerosene oil?
examples.solution:
Consider how these metals react.

  • Sodium and potassium are extremely reactive and react violently even with the moisture and oxygen of air.
  • Keeping them under kerosene oil cuts off air and moisture, preventing a dangerous reaction.
  • Answer: They are stored under kerosene because they react violently with air and water, and kerosene keeps these away.
examples.answer: They are stored under kerosene because they react violently with air and water, and kerosene keeps these away.

examples.problem: Example 3: What gas is released when zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, and how can it be tested?
examples.solution:
Recall the metal-acid reaction.

  • Most metals react with dilute acids to form a salt and release hydrogen gas.
  • Hydrogen burns with a characteristic "pop" sound when a lit splint is brought near it.
  • Answer: Hydrogen gas is released, and it is tested by the "pop" sound it makes with a burning splint.
examples.answer: Hydrogen gas is released, and it is tested by the "pop" sound it makes with a burning splint.

recap:
• Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides, which are generally basic (turn red litmus blue).
  • Metals react with water to release hydrogen; very reactive metals (sodium, potassium) react violently with cold water and are stored under kerosene.
  • Most metals react with dilute acids to form a salt and release hydrogen gas, which burns with a "pop".
  • The reactivity series arranges metals from most reactive (potassium, sodium) to least reactive (silver, gold).
  • A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from its salt solution; unreactive metals like gold resist reaction.

topics.title: Chemical Properties of Non-metals and Metalloids
topics.concept:
Just as metals have characteristic chemical properties, non-metals behave in their own typical ways, which are often the opposite of metals. Comparing the two helps complete our understanding of how elements react and explains many everyday observations, such as why burning sulphur or carbon produces acidic gases.

Reaction with oxygen: Non-metals react with oxygen to form non-metal oxides. The crucial difference from metals is that non-metal oxides are acidic (or neutral) in nature — they turn blue litmus red and form acids when dissolved in water. For example, carbon burns in oxygen to form carbon dioxide, which dissolves in water to give carbonic acid; sulphur burns to form sulphur dioxide, which forms sulphurous acid in water. (A few non-metal oxides, such as water and carbon monoxide, are neutral.) This is exactly why the gases released by burning fuels can cause acid rain.

Reaction with acids and water: Unlike most metals, non-metals generally do not react with dilute acids and do not displace hydrogen from them. Non-metals also do not usually react with water in the way reactive metals do. In terms of charge, non-metals tend to gain electrons in reactions, forming negative ions, whereas metals tend to lose electrons, forming positive ions — which is why metals and non-metals often combine to form compounds such as salts.

Between metals and non-metals lies a small group of elements called metalloids, which show intermediate properties — some metallic and some non-metallic. The most important examples are silicon (Si) and germanium (Ge) (boron and arsenic are others). Metalloids are often semiconductors, meaning they conduct electricity better than non-metals but not as well as metals. This special property makes silicon and germanium extremely valuable in making the chips and components of computers, mobile phones, and other electronic devices. Understanding non-metals and metalloids alongside metals shows how the whole range of elements provides materials for every kind of use, from acidic gases to the silicon chips of modern electronics.

examples.problem: Example 1: When carbon burns in oxygen, the oxide formed dissolves in water and turns blue litmus red. What is the nature of this oxide?
examples.solution:
Recall the nature of non-metal oxides.

  • Carbon is a non-metal, and non-metals form non-metal oxides.
  • Non-metal oxides are acidic, which is why the oxide turns blue litmus red.
  • Answer: The oxide (carbon dioxide) is acidic in nature.
examples.answer: The oxide (carbon dioxide) is acidic in nature.

examples.problem: Example 2: How does the reaction of non-metals with dilute acids differ from that of metals?
examples.solution:
Compare the two groups.

  • Most metals react with dilute acids to release hydrogen gas.
  • Non-metals generally do not react with dilute acids and do not release hydrogen.
  • Answer: Metals react with dilute acids to release hydrogen, but non-metals generally do not react with dilute acids.
examples.answer: Metals react with dilute acids to release hydrogen, but non-metals generally do not react with dilute acids.

examples.problem: Example 3: What is a metalloid, and why is silicon important in electronics?
examples.solution:
Recall the in-between group.

  • A metalloid is an element with properties between those of metals and non-metals, such as silicon.
  • Silicon is a semiconductor, conducting electricity moderately, which is ideal for electronic chips.
  • Answer: A metalloid has intermediate properties; silicon is a semiconductor, making it valuable for electronic chips and devices.
examples.answer: A metalloid has intermediate properties; silicon is a semiconductor, making it valuable for electronic chips and devices.

recap:
• Non-metals react with oxygen to form non-metal oxides, which are generally acidic (turn blue litmus red); a few are neutral.
  • The acidic gases from burning non-metal fuels (like sulphur and carbon) can cause acid rain.
  • Non-metals generally do not react with dilute acids and tend to gain electrons (forming negative ions), unlike metals.
  • Metalloids (e.g. silicon and germanium) have properties intermediate between metals and non-metals.
  • Metalloids are semiconductors and are widely used in computer chips, mobile phones, and electronic devices.

quiz.explanation: Non-metal oxides are generally acidic, turning blue litmus red.

quiz.q: Compared with metals, non-metals usually react with dilute acids:

quiz.explanation: Non-metals generally do not react with dilute acids, unlike metals.

quiz.explanation: Silicon is a metalloid and semiconductor used in electronic chips.

topics.title: Alloys
topics.concept:
Pure metals are useful, but they often lack the exact qualities we need — pure iron is comparatively soft and rusts easily, and pure gold is too soft for jewellery. To improve their properties, metals are frequently mixed with other metals or with non-metals. An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal with a small amount of a non-metal. Alloying is one of the oldest and most important techniques in technology, because it lets us tailor the strength, hardness, appearance, and resistance to corrosion of a material.

Alloys generally have better properties than the pure metals from which they are made. They are often harder and stronger, more resistant to corrosion (rusting), and may have a more attractive appearance or a lower melting point, depending on what is added. This is why most metals we use in daily life are actually alloys rather than pure metals.

Several alloys are especially important. Steel is an alloy of iron with a small amount of carbon; it is far stronger and harder than pure iron and is used for construction, tools, and machinery. Stainless steel is steel with added chromium and nickel, which makes it resistant to rusting — ideal for cutlery, utensils, and surgical instruments. Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, valued for its golden colour and used in decorative items, utensils, and musical instruments. Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin, which is hard and durable and was historically used for tools, statues, and medals.

Alloys are found everywhere around us. The pots in our kitchens, the bodies of vehicles, coins, jewellery (gold is alloyed with copper to harden it), aircraft (light, strong aluminium alloys), and electrical fittings all rely on alloys chosen for the right combination of properties. By understanding alloys, we see how mixing materials cleverly produces substances better suited to human needs than any single pure metal.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is an alloy, and why are alloys made?
examples.solution:
Consider the definition and purpose.

  • An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal with a small amount of a non-metal.
  • Alloys are made because they have better properties (such as strength and corrosion resistance) than pure metals.
  • Answer: An alloy is a mixture of metals (or a metal with a non-metal), made to improve properties like strength and corrosion resistance.
examples.answer: An alloy is a mixture of metals (or a metal with a non-metal), made to improve properties like strength and corrosion resistance.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name the components of (a) brass and (b) bronze.
examples.solution:
Recall the composition of each alloy.

  • Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.
  • Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin.
  • Answer: (a) Brass = copper + zinc; (b) Bronze = copper + tin.
examples.answer: (a) Brass = copper + zinc; (b) Bronze = copper + tin.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why is stainless steel used to make cutlery and surgical instruments rather than ordinary iron?
examples.solution:
Compare the resistance to rust.

  • Stainless steel is steel with chromium and nickel added, which makes it resistant to rusting.
  • Cutlery and surgical instruments are exposed to water and must stay clean and rust-free.
  • Answer: Stainless steel resists rusting, so it keeps cutlery and surgical instruments clean and durable, unlike ordinary iron.
examples.answer: Stainless steel resists rusting, so it keeps cutlery and surgical instruments clean and durable, unlike ordinary iron.

recap:
• An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal with a small amount of a non-metal.
  • Alloys usually have better properties than pure metals — harder, stronger, and more corrosion-resistant.
  • Steel = iron + carbon (strong, used in construction and tools).
  • Stainless steel = iron + chromium + nickel (rust-resistant, used in cutlery and instruments).
  • Brass = copper + zinc; Bronze = copper + tin — used in utensils, decorative items, statues, and medals.

quiz.explanation: An alloy mixes two or more metals, or a metal with a small amount of a non-metal.

topics.title: Corrosion and its Prevention
topics.concept:
When metals are exposed to air, moisture, and other substances over time, their surfaces are slowly eaten away and damaged. This gradual eating away of a metal by the action of air, moisture, and chemicals in the surroundings is called corrosion. Corrosion is a chemical change in which the metal reacts with substances in its environment to form new compounds on its surface. It is a serious problem because it weakens metal structures and causes enormous losses of useful material every year.

Different metals corrode in different ways. The most familiar example is the rusting of iron, in which iron exposed to both water and oxygen forms a reddish-brown layer of rust (hydrated iron oxide). Other metals corrode too: silver tarnishes, forming a dull black coating when it reacts with sulphur compounds in the air; copper develops a green coating (called verdigris) over time; and even aluminium forms a thin oxide layer, though in aluminium's case this layer actually protects the metal underneath from further corrosion.

Corrosion can be prevented or slowed in several ways, mostly by keeping air and moisture away from the metal surface or by using less reactive coatings. Common methods include painting (used for gates, railings, and bridges), applying oil or grease (for tools and machine parts), galvanisation — coating iron with a layer of zinc — and electroplating, in which a thin layer of a less reactive metal such as chromium, nickel, or tin is deposited on the surface. Another important method is alloying, such as making stainless steel, which resists corrosion because of the chromium and nickel it contains.

Preventing corrosion is highly practical and economically important. It protects bridges, vehicles, ships, pipelines, machinery, tools, and household items, keeping them safe and extending their life, and it saves the huge amounts of money that would otherwise be lost to replacing corroded metal. Choosing the right prevention method for each situation — paint for large structures, galvanising for pipes and sheets, electroplating for taps and decorative fittings, and stainless steel for utensils — completes our understanding of how we make the most of metals while protecting them from being destroyed by their surroundings.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is corrosion, and what type of change is it?
examples.solution:
Define the process and classify it.

  • Corrosion is the gradual eating away of a metal by the action of air, moisture, and chemicals in its surroundings.
  • The metal reacts to form new compounds on its surface, so a new substance is formed.
  • Answer: Corrosion is the slow eating away of a metal by its surroundings, and it is a chemical change.
examples.answer: Corrosion is the slow eating away of a metal by its surroundings, and it is a chemical change.

examples.problem: Example 2: Silver ornaments turn black after some time. What is this process called, and why does it happen?
examples.solution:
Identify the type of corrosion in silver.

  • Silver reacts with sulphur compounds present in the air to form a dull black coating.
  • This corrosion of silver is called tarnishing.
  • Answer: It is called tarnishing; it happens because silver reacts with sulphur compounds in the air to form a black coating.
examples.answer: It is called tarnishing; it happens because silver reacts with sulphur compounds in the air to form a black coating.

examples.problem: Example 3: How does galvanisation prevent the corrosion of iron?
examples.solution:
Recall what galvanisation does.

  • Galvanisation coats the iron object with a protective layer of zinc.
  • This zinc layer keeps air and moisture away from the iron and resists corrosion itself.
  • Answer: Galvanisation coats iron with zinc, which keeps out air and moisture and prevents the iron from corroding.
examples.answer: Galvanisation coats iron with zinc, which keeps out air and moisture and prevents the iron from corroding.

recap:
• Corrosion is the gradual eating away of a metal by air, moisture, and chemicals in the surroundings; it is a chemical change.
  • Rusting of iron (needing water and oxygen) is the commonest corrosion; silver tarnishes black and copper develops a green coating.
  • Corrosion weakens structures and causes large economic losses.
  • Prevention methods include painting, oiling/greasing, galvanisation (zinc coating), and electroplating (chromium, nickel, tin).
  • Alloying, such as making stainless steel, also resists corrosion; the method is chosen to suit each use.
